          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
2. Mr.C.S. Vaidyanathan and Mr.Vikramjit Banerjee, the learned
senior counsel appearing for the NABARD,  submitted that NABARD
is ready and willing to pay an amount of Rs.66.76 crore to the
12

--- Page 107 ---
SLP(C)  No.16087/2017
Bank.  This amount would be towards 15,586 loan accounts in the
name of different farmers who were declared ineligible under the
Scheme.
3. Both the learned senior counsel would submit that this
figure has been determined in consultation with the Bank.
However, the learned senior counsel appearing for the bank would
dispute such statement being made on behalf of the NABARD.
According to the learned senior counsel appearing for the Bank
there has been no consultation so far with NABARD for the
purpose of determining the exact amount. 
4. Let the subsequent developments be placed on record by way
of an affidavit at the earliest duly affirmed by a responsible
officer of NABARD.  The affidavit should indicate in what manner
this  amount  of  Rs.66.76  crore  has  been  determined.   The
affidavit should also indicate on what basis the bank has
determined this amount.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant to the detailed order passed by us on 18.08.2026,
constituting a High-Powered Enquiry Committee (HPEC) and providing
detailed directions on the issues to be considered by it, parties
on either side have filed a number of affidavits and applications.
Consequently, in the course of the proceedings, a multitude of
contentions  and  suggestions  were  placed  before  us  for  our
consideration. 
2. At the very outset, we have been informed by the Union of
India that they have complied with paragraph 24 of our order dated
18.08,2026, in so far as providing infrastructure and facilities to
the HPEC is concerned.
3. That being so, I.A. No. 258046/2026 has been filed on behalf
of some of the Petitioners, seeking reconstitution of the HPEC.
Having perused the contents of the aforesaid application, we are
constrained  to  observe,  with  some  measure  of  disquiet,  that
aspersions have been cast upon the HPEC in a manner that is both
premature and precipitate.
4. In the circumstances, we are not inclined to effect any
alteration in the constitution of the Committee, particularly where
the prayer for such reconstitution proceeds on nothing more than
conjecture and preconceived notions, articulated even before the
9

--- Page 118 ---
HPEC has embarked upon its enquiry.  It must be understood by one
and all that the HPEC has been constituted to assist this Court
with the highest standards of fairness and transparency and with a
dispassionate approach. The HPEC is not created to espouse the
causes of one or the other party before us.
5. Be that as it may, we have the parties on either side on a
myriad of other issues and in that regard, deem it necessary to
pass the following directions and clarifications in supplementation
to the directions passed on 18.08.2026:
i. At the risk of reiteration, we request that the HPEC may,
in the first instance, proceed with its enquiry into the
issues  enumerated  at  items  (i),  (vi),  and  (vii)  of
paragraph 12, and item (iii) of paragraph 13 of our order
dated 18.08.2026. This would include the issues pertaining
to the use of pellet guns, the targeted violence and
harassment of female protestors, as well as the issue of
excessive violence and destruction of property occasioned
on either side;
ii. We further reiterate the caveat entered by us in paragraph
19 of our order dated 18.08.2026, regarding the broader
constitutional questions arising herein, and reaffirm that
the  same  shall  be  considered  by  this  Court  at  the
appropriate stage;
10

--- Page 119 ---
iii. With respect to the concerns voiced over the treatment of
witnesses, and of those who may wish to come forward before
the  HPEC  to  furnish  their  account  and  voice  their
grievances,  we  request  the  HPEC  that  such  vulnerable
witnesses be extended due protection and their identities
be kept confidential and undisclosed, in furtherance of
paragraph 20 of our order dated 18.08.2026;
iv. It goes without saying that utmost confidentiality shall be
maintained in respect of any statements given or evidence
submitted by such vulnerable witnesses to the HPEC. In
furtherance  thereof,  a  separate  online  portal  may  be
created to facilitate such witnesses and other requisite
stakeholders to submit their documents and evidence;
v. We clarify that the role of the nodal counsel appointed by
us in paragraph 21 of the order dated 18.08.2026 shall be
confined to rendering assistance to this Court in the
course of the instant proceedings. A large part of their
support shall be logistical in nature, extended to this
Court and is not to be construed as constituting a line of
communication between the HPEC, this Court, and the parties
before us;
vi. We have also been informed that the nodal counsel have not
been furnished with the paperbooks and other material
11

--- Page 120 ---
relevant to the instant proceedings. The Registry of this
Court is accordingly directed to remedy the same at the
earliest;
vii. In this vein, we deem it appropriate to appoint Dr. Monika
Gusain, Senior Advocate, along with Mr. C. Solomon, AOR, as
learned  Amici  Curiae , who shall assist this Court as a
representative of the HPEC, and shall further act as an
independent arbiter between the parties;
viii. Similarly, we also request the HPEC to appoint a Member
Secretary at the earliest, so as to facilitate any such
logistical or other secretarial assistance as the HPEC may
require in the discharge of its functions. The same has
already been expressed at paragraph 26 of our earlier
order; 
ix. Keeping  these  directions  and  clarifications  in  mind,
together with those already issued vide our order dated
18.08.2026, we request the HPEC to submit its first report
to this Court at the earliest.
6. Specifically in WP(Crl) No.324/2026, vehement submissions were
canvassed as to the vulnerability of one particular young female
protestor, who is stated to be a child of fourteen years of age. It
was contended that several threats have been made to her life, as
well as to that of her family, occasioning grave and continuing
12

--- Page 121 ---
apprehension as to the safety of both her and her family. It was
further contended that no action has been taken by the Delhi Police
against the miscreant(s) who have allegedly carried out such
attacks upon her and her family, a lapse that has only compounded
the risks attendant upon securing her safety.
7. In this light, we direct the Delhi Police to assess the threat
perception and provide the necessary protection to the said child
and her family so as to secure her safety, and to expeditiously
conduct an investigation against such anti-social elements who are
allegedly threatening or harassing her and her family. Let a status
report be filed by the Delhi Police in this behalf before the next
date of hearing.
8. Ordered accordingly.
9. List on 09.10.2026 for further consideration.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

NON-REPORTABLE 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 2400 OF 2014  
 
STATE OF HIMACHAL 
PRADESH                 ….APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
SULENDER                       ….RESPONDENT(S) 
J U D G M E N T 
1. Heard. 
2. The State of Himachal Pradesh is in appeal 
before us, assailing the judgment dated 22 nd April, 
2014 rendered by the High Court of Himachal 
Pradesh1 whereby the Division Bench, accepted the 
appeal against conviction filed by the accused-
Sulender and set aside the judgment dated 21st May, 
2008 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Fast 
Track Court, Shimla 2 in Sessions Trial No. 17 -R of 
2008/07 whereby the respondent had been convicted 
for the offence punishable under Section 302 of the 
Indian Penal Code, 1860 3 and was sentenced to 
 
1 Hereinafter, referred to as “High Court”. 
2 Hereinafter, referred to as “trial Court”. 
3 For short, “IPC”. 

--- Page 173 ---
2 
 
undergo rigorous imprisonment for life a long with a 
fine of Rs.20,000/-. The Division Bench of the High 
Court, acquitted the accused of the charge of 
committing the murder of his own wife Smt. Devki on 
27th June, 2006.   
3. In brief, the prosecution case is that the 
respondent and his wife Smt. Devki (since deceased) 
were working as labourers in the construction work 
of the school building of which Krishan Kumar (PW -
5) was the Contractor.   
4. The respondent-Sulender appeared at the Police 
Station, Chirgaon on 27 th June, 2006 and made a 
complaint that he and his wife had gone into the open 
to answer the call of nature. His wife was standing on 
the roadside whereas he went to the valley side.  
While he was in the process of easing himself, he 
heard the cries of his wife but when he came back on 
the road, she was not to be seen anywhere. Despite 
making a fervent search near the road and the 
riverside, when he could not trace his wife, he 
returned to camp and there too, did not find his wife 
present. He suspected that his wife had gone missing 
with a co-labourer. On this report of the respondent, 

--- Page 174 ---
3 
 
a missing person report  (Exhibit PW15/A)  was 
registered at the police station. 
5. The prosecution has come out with a totally 
different story, alleging that, as a matter of fact, the 
accused had taken his wife to the jungle in the early 
hours of morning on the pretext of having sexual 
intercourse with her.  She was made to lie down and 
instead of performing sexual intercourse, the 
respondent ass aulted her with a knife and caused 
injuries on her stomach, head and other parts of the 
body thereby killing her. He then lifted her clothes 
upwards and covered the body with the shawl and 
returned to the camp. The prosecution further claims 
that while the respondent was returning to the camp, 
he was seen by Brahma Nand (PW -13) at a distance 
of about 500 meters from the place of occurrence. 
6. The trial Court concluded that the prosecution 
had established the guilt of the accused by leading a 
complete chain of circumstantial evidence which 
pointed to the guilt of the respondent alone. These 
circumstances were comprised of last seen together, 
recovery of the weapon of the offence in furtherance 
of the disclosure made by the respondent , and the 

--- Page 175 ---
4 
 
extra judicial confession made before Surender Singh 
(PW-1) and Pyare Lal (PW-4). 
7. In appeal, the High Court found that 
circumstance No. 1, i.e., the last seen together , was 
not proved by the prosecution. Two co -labourers 
Vikas and his wife Pyari Devi were  cited by the 
prosecution in the list of witnesses to prove this fact 
but both of them were not examined  at the trial . 
Hence, the High Court concluded that there was no 
evidence on record to show that the respondent and 
the deceased had gone together from the camp at 
4.30 a.m. The missing person report (Exhibit 
PW15/A) lodged by the respondent was admitted, but 
as per this report, the respondent and his wife went 
out at about 6.00 a.m. to answer the call of nature. 
8. The High Court further found that the dead 
body was found at a place about 4 to 5 kilometres 
away from the dera/camp and there could not be any 
reason as to why the respondent and his wife would  
go to such a distant place for answering the call of 
nature. Thus, the High Court was of the view that the 
allegation of last seen together was doubtful and not 
proved on account of non-examination of the material 
witnesses.  

--- Page 176 ---
5 
 
9. The 2nd circumstance relied upon by the 
prosecution was pertaining to the alleged suspicious 
conduct of the respondent, which was allegedly 
observed by Brahma Nand (PW-13). The High Court 
noticed that the only aspersion which Brahma Nand 
(PW-13) made in his evidence was that he had seen 
one person walking briskly , having covered himself 
with a grey shawl. However, the fact remains that 
Brahma Nand (PW-13) did not identify the accused to 
be the said suspicious person. The High Court 
further found that the mere fact that the witness (PW-
13) had seen the suspect walking briskly, that, by 
itself, could not be treated to be an incriminating 
circumstance and had no consequence on the case of 
the prosecution.   
10. The 3rd circumstance, being the soiling of the 
clothes of the respondent by the stains of the soil , 
was held to be inconsequential because admittedly 
the respondent was present at the spot with the 
police when the dead body was discovered. The High 
Court held that it was absolutely natural that the 
respondent would have assisted in lifting the dead 
body of his wife and in this process, he may have got 
the stain s of soil  on his clothes.  Hence, in our 

--- Page 177 ---
6 
 
opinion, the said circumstance was also rightly held 
to be not proved against the respondent and correctly 
discarded.  
11. The 4th circumstance was the alleged extra 
judicial confession made by the respondent in the 
presence of Pyare Lal (PW-4). In this regard, the High 
Court considered the evidence of the material 
witnesses and found that the alleged extra judicial 
confession was made by the accused when PW -4 
questioned him at the instance of the police. The High 
Court also found that when the extra judicial 
confession was allegedly made, the respondent was 
in physical custody of the police , though his formal 
arrest was shown later and hence, the extra judicial 
confession could not be admitted in evidence.   
12. The last circumstance was the recovery of the 
knife. Suffice it to say that the High Court found 
various lacunae in the evidence of the material 
witnesses who deposed about the recovery of the 
knife. Further, th e High Court found that the FSL 
report did not connect the recovered knife with the 
commission of the crime  as no opinion of matching 
blood group was given by the FSL. 

--- Page 178 ---
7 
 
13. The High Court also took note of the fact that 
the prosecution could not prove that the respondent 
had any motive to murder his own wife. Concluding 
thus, the High Court proceeded to acquit the 
respondent of the charges  by the impugned 
judgment. 
14. Having heard learned counsel for the appellant-
State and considering the material placed on record, 
we are in complete agreement with the reasons 
assigned by the High Court in the impugned 
judgment whereby the respondent was acquitted of 
the charges. The circumstances sought to be relied 
upon by the prosecution as being incriminating 
against the responden t were neither proved by 
convincing evidence nor were the said circumstances 
of such a nature which could form a complete 
incriminating chain pointing exclusively to the guilt 
of the respondent.   
15. Law is well settled by a catena of decisions 
rendered by this Court 4 that, where two views are 
possible, one favouring the prosecution and the other 
favouring the accused, the appellate Court, while 
 
4 See, Chandrappa & Ors. v. State of Karnataka, (2007) 4 SCC 415. 

--- Page 179 ---
8 
 
exercising jurisdiction in an appeal against acquittal, 
should adopt the view favourable to the accused and 
refrain from interfering with the judgment of acquittal 
unless such judgment suffers from patent perversity.  
16. In the present case, having gone through the 
judgment rendered by the High Court, the judgment 
rendered by the trial Court and the evidence placed 
on record, we are of the view that the prosecution has 
fallen woefully short of bringing home the guilt of the 
respondent by evidence which is conclusive and 
points exclusively to the guilt of the respondent. The 
impugned judgment dated 22nd April, 2014 does not 
suffer from any infirmity warranting interference. 
17. Hence, the appeal lacks merit and is accordingly 
dismissed as such.  
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand 
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This contempt petition has been filed alleging willful and
deliberate violation of the judgment of this Court dated 30.01.2025
passed in Civil Appeal No.1297 of 2025 ( Parimal Kumar & ors. vs.
State of Jharkhand & ors.) . The operative portion of the judgment
and order dated 30.01.2025 is as under:
(i) The impugned judgment of the High Court
permitting the candidates of CTET and STET
holders of neighbouring States to participate
in ongoing selection process to the post of
4

--- Page 184 ---
Assistant  Teacher  of  Primary  and  Upper
Primary schools pursuant to Advertisement No.
13 stands set-aside;
(ii) The JTET holders who were possessing the
requisite  qualification  under  the  2022
Recruitment  Rules,  prior  to  the  2024
Amendment and participated shall be eligible
for appointment and their result be declared
forthwith  and  the  appointments  be  made
strictly on merit;
(iii) We make it clear that CTET holders or
STET  holders,  who  have  applied  after  the
judgment of the High Court or after amendment
in the rules or advertisement would not be
eligible for the recruitment in furtherance
to the Advertisement No. 13/2023.
2. In the proceedings held on 19.05.2026, this Court clarified in
paragraph 18 of the said order that reserved candidates who come in
the merit list prepared for unreserved posts shall be included
merit wise if their marks are above the unreserved candidates.
Therefore, the migration of a candidate of the reserved category
who secured higher marks is permitted to the unreserved category.
2.1 However, an opportunity was granted to the Staff Selection
Commission to file a fresh reply indicating compliance to the
directions of this Court.
3. Now, the Staff Selection Commission has given an explanation.
4. There appears to be convergence of views between the Staff
Selection Commission and the Government of Jharkhand; both are
relying on an administrative office memorandum dated  31.10.2012
regarding clarification for granting exemptions and concessions to
5

--- Page 185 ---
candidates  belonging  to  the  reserved  category  during  direct
recruitment. As per the office memorandum, when the selection of
reserved  category  candidates  is  made  by  providing
exemptions/concessions  in  the  upper  age  limit,  experience,
educational qualification, number of attempts to appear in written
examination as compared to general category candidates and extended
zone of consideration area is done on the basis thereof, then they
will be adjusted only against the vacancies of the concerned
reserved category. Such candidates shall be deemed unavailable for
the unreserved vacancies.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the State of Jharkhand submits
that this office memorandum was issued on the basis of office
memorandum dated 01.07.1998 of the Central Government. Prima facie
such office memorandum is completely untenable, being contrary to
the law laid down by this Court in several judgments including in
Chhaya vs. State of Maharashtra  (2026 SC OnLine SC 457). In Chhaya,
the  appellants  before  this  Court  belonging  to  the  reserved
category, though more meritorious than the last selected candidate
under the general category were excluded from the merit list on the
ground that they had availed the relaxation in qualifying marks in
the teachers’ eligibility test. This Court clarified and declared
that the appellants who were admittedly more meritorious than the
last selected candidate under the general category cannot be
excluded from consideration under the general category in the
absence  of  any  express  prohibition  in  the  recruitment
rules/notification. The relaxation in qualifying criteria only
affects eligibility and not merit and migration is permissible in
6

--- Page 186 ---
the  absence  of  prohibition.  In  the  facts  of  that  case,  a
declaration was made that the appellants were entitled to migrate
to general category.
6. An endeavor has been made to show that the aforesaid two
office memoranda are in the nature of prohibition and, supports the
proposition that more meritorious reserved category candidates
cannot migrate to the general category.
7. The notification referred to in Chhaya in our understanding
must be of a statutory character because the same has been referred
to in the context of recruitment rules. Without any statutory
prohibition  or  exclusion,  more  meritorious  reserved  category
candidates  cannot  be  excluded  from  migrating  to  the  general
category by way of an administrative instruction.
8. That apart, in our order dated 19.05.2026 in paragraph 23 we
have clarified that the plea of non-availability of vacancies is
not germane in as much as in all the categories vacancies are
available.
9. We, therefore, direct the State of Jharkhand through the
concerned officers to implement the judgment and order of this
Court dated  19.01.2025 within a period of 4 weeks from today,
failing which the concerned officials will expose themselves to
contempt proceedings before this Court. 
10. Let a compliance affidavit be filed by the Chief Secretary to
the Government of Jharkhand within 6 weeks from today.
11. Impleadment Application bearing I.A. No.184711/2026 stands
dismissed.
12. Diary No.43106/2025 may be de-tagged and listed separately.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).  406 & 407 of 2012 
 
 
  
MANJAPPA & ANR. ETC.      …APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
 
STATE OF KARNATAKA R/BY  
ARASIKERE POLICE   …RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
 
 
O R D E R  
 
1. The present appeals challenge the judgment and 
order dated 05.08.2010 (impugned order) passed by the 
High Court of Karnataka, Bangalore, whereby the judgment 
of acquittal dated 26.12.2004 passed by the Additional 
Sessions Judge and Presiding Officer, Fast Track Court-I 
has been reversed, resulting in the conviction of offence 
under Section 148 and 304 Part II of the Indian Penal Code, 
1860 (IPC) apart from the fine, in default, against the 
present appellant(s). 

--- Page 189 ---
 
2 
2. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant(s) has 
brought to the notice of this Court that appellant No. 1, 
Manjappa has since expired, and therefore, the appeal qua 
him stands abated. Ordered accordingly. 
3. As regards the judgment which is impugned herein, 
learned counsel appearing for the appellant(s) asserts that 
the High Court has exceeded its limits and has not come to 
a conclusion that the findings  as recorded resulting in 
acquittal of the appellant(s) were perverse and except 
findings of guilt, the conclusions as drawn by the Trial 
Court are unsustainable. On this legal issue itself which is 
based upon the settled principle of law, the learned counsel 
asserts that the impugned judgment deserves to be set 
aside. 
4. Apart from this aspect, the learned counsel has 
pressed upon the fact that the prosecution has been unable 
to prove the case against the accused/appellant(s), and 
therefore, the findings as recorded by the Trial Court are 
fully justified, which should not have been interfered with 
by the High Court. He, therefore, prays for setting aside of 
the impugned judgment and restoring the acquittal of the 
appellant(s). 

--- Page 190 ---
 
3 
5. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing for the 
respondent-State has opposed the prayer as has been made 
by the learned counsel for the appellant(s) and has asserted 
that the High Court has gone into each and every aspect 
with regard to the role, the act and the evidence which has 
been brought on record by the prosecution. The evidence 
having been dealt with clearly establishes the guilt of the 
accused/appellant(s) and has rightly come to the 
conclusion that the acquittal is not in accordance with law 
and thus, the judgment deserves to be upheld. 
6. We have considered the submissions advanced by the 
learned counsel(s) appearing for the parties and have gone 
through the impugned judgment of the High Court. It is a 
settled proposition of law that for interfering in the 
judgment of acquittal, a finding has to be recorded by the 
Appellate Court that there is perversity in the findings as 
has been recorded by the Trial Court while granting 
acquittal and that the said findings are based on wrong 
appreciation of evidence. Apart from that, a specific 
assertion has to be made and concluded that except for the 
finding of guilt, no other conclusion could have been drawn. 
That apart, it is also settled that  when two views are 

--- Page 191 ---
 
4 
possible of which one has been taken by the Trial Court, no 
interference is called for in a criminal appeal preferred 
against the order of the acquittal. 
7. In the case of “Constable 907 Surendra Singh & Anr. V 
State of Uttarakhand1”, a Bench of this Court to which one 
of us was a member (Augustine George Masih, J.) in para 
no. 11 has summarised this legal position and observed as 
follows: 
“11. Recently, in the case of Babu Sahebagouda Redragoudar 
and others v. State of Karnataka, a Bench of this Court to 
which one of us was a Member (B.R. Gavai, J.) had an 
occasion to consider the legal position with regard to the 
scope of interference in an appeal against acquittal. It was 
observed thus: 
 
38. First of all, we would like to reiterate the principles laid 
down by this Court governing the scope of interference by 
the High Court in an appeal filed by the State for 
challenging acquittal of the accused recorded by the trial 
court. 
 
39. This Court in Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar [Rejesh 
Prasad v. State of Bihar, (2022) 3 SCC 471 : (2002) 2 SCC 
(Cri) 371] encapsulated the legal position covering the field 
after considering various earlier judgments and held as 
below : (SCC pp. 482-83, para 29) 
 
29. After referring to a catena of judgments, this Court 
culled out the following general principles regarding the 
powers of the appellate court while dealing with an 
appeal against an order of acquittal in the following 
words : (Chandrappa case [Chandrappa v. State of 
Karnataka, (2007) 4 SCC 415 : (2007) 2 SCC (Cri) 325] , 
SCC p. 432, para 42)  
 
‘42. From the above decisions, in our considered view, 
the following general principles regarding powers of 
 
1  2025 INSC 114 

--- Page 192 ---
 
5 
the appellate court while dealing with an appeal 
against an order of acquittal emerge: 
 
(1) An appellate court has full power to review, 
reappreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which 
the order of acquittal is founded.  
 
(2) The Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 puts no 
limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such 
power and an appellate court on the evidence before 
it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of 
fact and of law.  
 
(3) Various expressions, such as, “substantial and 
compelling reasons”, “good and sufficient grounds”, 
“very strong circumstances”, “distorted conclusions”, 
“glaring mistakes”, etc. are not intended to curtail 
extensive powers of an appellate court in an appeal 
against acquittal. Such phraseologies are more in the 
nature of “flourishes of language” to emphasise the 
reluctance of an appellate court to interfere with 
acquittal than to curtail the power of the court to 
review the evidence and to come to its own 
conclusion. 
 
(4) An appellate court, however, must bear in mind 
that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption 
in favour of the accused. Firstly, the presumption of 
innocence is available to him under the fundamental 
principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person 
shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved 
guilty by a competent court of law. Secondly, the 
accused having secured his acquittal, the 
presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, 
reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court.  
 
(5) If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the 
basis of the evidence on record, the appellate court 
should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded 
by the trial court.’ ”  
 
40. Further, in H.D. Sundara v. State of Karnataka [H.D. 
Sundara v. State of Karnataka, (2023) 9 SCC 581: (2023) 3 
SCC (Cri) 748] this Court summarised the principles 
governing the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while 
dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 
378CrPC as follows : (SCC p. 584, para 8)  
 
“8. … 8.1. The acquittal of the accused further 
strengthens the presumption of innocence;  
 

--- Page 193 ---
 
6 
8.2. The appellate court, while hearing an appeal 
against acquittal, is entitled to reappreciate the oral and 
documentary evidence;  
 
8.3. The appellate court, while deciding an appeal 
against acquittal, after reappreciating the evidence, is 
required to consider whether the view taken by the trial 
court is a possible view which could have been taken on 
the basis of the evidence on record;  
 
8.4. If the view taken is a possible view, the appellate 
court cannot overturn the order of acquittal on the 
ground that another view was also possible; and  
 
8.5. The appellate court can interfere with the order of 
acquittal only if it comes to a finding that the only 
conclusion which can be recorded on the basis of the 
evidence on record was that the guilt of the accused was 
proved beyond a reasonable doubt and no other 
conclusion was possible.”  
 
41. Thus, it is beyond the pale of doubt that the scope of 
interference by an appellate court for reversing the 
judgment of acquittal recorded by the trial court in favour 
of the accused has to be exercised within the four corners 
of the following principles: 
 
41.1. That the judgment of acquittal suffers from patent 
perversity;  
 
41.2. That the same is based on a misreading/omission to 
consider material evidence on record; and  
 
41.3. That no two reasonable views are possible and only 
the view consistent with the guilt of the accused is possible 
from the evidence available on record.” 
 
12. It could thus be seen that it is a settled legal position that 
the interference with the finding of acquittal recorded by the 
learned trial judge would be warranted by the High Court 
only if the judgment of acquittal suffers from patent 
perversity; that the same is based on a misreading/omission 
to consider material evidence on record; and that no two 
reasonable views are possible and only the view consistent 
with the guilt of the accused is possible from the evidence 
available on record.” 
 
On perusal of the judgment impugned, we do not find any 

--- Page 194 ---
 
7 
mention or any reference in this regard by the High Court. 
The basic principles, on which interference in an appeal is 
to be based and sustained having been not gone into, the 
judgment as passed by the Appellate Court cannot sustain 
and deserves to be set aside on this short ground alone. 
8. We have gone through judgment of acquittal dated 
26.12.2004 passed by the Trial Court and find that the view 
as taken therein could have been taken on the basis of the 
evidence on record and is thus a possible view. The Appellate 
Court was therefore not justified in overturning the order of 
acquittal on the ground that another view was also possible. 
The interference therefore by the High Court is not justified. 
9. It may also be observed here that guilt has been found 
qua the accused to be under Section 304 Part II IPC, 
simplicitor, and there is no finding with regard to there 
being an offence having been committed under Section 149 
of the IPC. If that be so, there has to be finding with regard 
to the specific injury having been caused by a particular 
person/accused. There has to be specific role attributed 
and found to have been so committed by the accused 
concerned, which is missing. On this ground also, the 
judgment cannot sustain. 

--- Page 195 ---
 
8 
10. In view of the above, the appeals are allowed. The 
impugned judgment and order dated 05.08.2010 passed by 
the High Court are hereby set aside and the judgment of the 
Trial Court is restored. 
11. Accused/appellants are acquitted of the charges. The 
appellant(s) are on bail, and therefore, need not surrender. 
Their bail bonds stand discharged. 
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
 
 
....................,J. 
     (AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No. 12952 of 2026
(@ Special Leave Petition (Civil) No.   26428 of 2025)  
MADHURI KUMAR        APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
KARAN KAPOOR       RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL No(s). 12953-12954 of 2026
(@ Special Leave Petition (Civil) No(s). 33896-33897   of 2025)  
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant Madhuri Kumar is the landlady. She is
aggrieved by paragraph No.86 of the impugned judgment and
order dated 19.08.2025 passed by the High Court of Delhi
at New Delhi (briefly ‘the High Court’ hereinafter),
disposing of 02 petitions filed by the respondent-tenant
Karan Kapoor under Article 227 of the Constitution of
India.
4. The landlady has filed Civil Suit No.867 of 2018 for
recovery of possession, arrears of rent and mesne profit
from her tenant. In the meanwhile, the tenant has also
filed a suit contending that there was an agreement to
sell the tenanted premises to him. Since the agreement was
not being acted upon, he has filed a suit for specific
performance of contract, being CS (OS) No.397 of 2019.
1

--- Page 204 ---
5. Both  the  suits  are  being  presently  being  heard
together.
6. The respondent-tenant had challenged the order dated
29.11.2022 in CM (M) 1437/2022 and had further challenged
orders dated 27.07.2023 and 04.09.2023 in CM(M) 1786/2023
before the High Court.
7. By  order  dated  29.11.2022,  the  Trial  Court  had
directed the defendant (tenant) to pay, by way of cheque
or demand draft, the entire arrear rental amount including
interest till 13.09.2022; further he was directed to pay,
through  cheque  or  demand  draft,  a  further  sum  of
Rs.3,89,061/- which had become due upto 13.10.2022 with
simple interest at the rate of 6% per annum; and a further
sum of Rs.3,89,061/-, which had become due on 13.11.2022
with simple interest at the rate of 6% per annum.
7.1.In respect of the rent/user charges which had become
due on 13.12.2022, the defendant (tenant) was directed to
pay the aforesaid amount by way of cheque or demand draft.
8. By  the  order  dated  27.07.2023,  the  Trial  Court
dismissed the application filed by the defendant (tenant)
for securing his interest in the monthly rentals from
December, 2022 to February, 2023.
9. By order dated 04.09.2023, the Trial Court directed
the defendant (tenant) to make payment of whatever amount
was due towards rent to the plaintiff as mentioned by her
in her application under Order XV-A of the Civil Procedure
2

--- Page 205 ---
Code, 1908, within one month, failing which it was stated
that the defence of the defendant would be struck off.
10. By the impugned judgment and order dated 19.08.2025,
the High Court noted the following:
“81. Fact  remains  that  merely  because
tenant  has  filed  a  suit  for  specific
performance, he cannot be permitted to wriggle
out  of  his  obligation  to  pay  rentals/user
charges. The tenant has, merely, come up with
hypothetical propositions and cannot earn any
compassion,  merely  on  the  basis  of  some
fanciful speculation. Moreover, he can always
make appropriate submissions in this regard in
said two suits at the stage of final arguments
and suitable directions can always be passed,
in  synchronization  with  the  eventual  final
outcome.
82. Therefore,  his  demand  to  stall  and
suspend  further  payment,  unless  landlady
furnishes  bank  guarantee,  is  completely
specious. As noted already, if future rentals
are hurting him, he being, a mere tenant at
sufferance, can always leave the premises.”
11. Having  said  that,  the  High  Court  surprisingly
modified the orders of the Trial Court in the following
manner:
“86. Resultantly,  both  the  abovesaid
petitions are disposed of in aforesaid terms
and the impugned orders stand modified to the
extent that there would not be any further
increase  in  the  user  charges  beyond  Rs.
4,70,764/- per month and it would remain static
at said rate, till the final adjudication of
3

--- Page 206 ---
the  suits  and  further  that  the  înterest
component, already paid, would be liable to be
set off or adjusted from the future payments.”
12. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
considering the reasonings of the High Court, the abrupt
modification of the Trial Court’s order does not stand to
reason. Further, we feel that freezing the user charges at
Rs.4,70,764/- per month till final disposal of the two
suits, does not appear to be just and proper. It should
best be left to the Trial Court to take a decision as the
suit progresses. The only reason given by the High Court
to justify freezing of the user charges is found in
paragraph No.58 which reads as follows:
“58.  Fact  remains  that  this  Court,  while
exercising supervisory powers, would not go
into the aforesaid factual aspect as to what
would  be  the  present  rent  of  a  similarly
situated property in the area in question. It
is entirely upto the parties to lead evidence
in order to demonstrate its respective stance
with respect to prevalent rent but since the
user  charges  have  already  reached  Rs.
4,70,764/-,  this  Court  feels  that  increase
cannot be permitted to be there in perpetuity
and for an indefinite period and, therefore,
till the suit is finally adjudicated, let there
be no further increase in the user charges,
beyond Rs. 4,70,764/-.”
13. As noted supra, we do not concur with the view taken
by the High Court. Increase in user charges, annually or
4

--- Page 207 ---
otherwise, is neither unusual nor uncommon. It is for the
Trial Court to take a decision as and when application(s)
are filed for increase of the user charges. We express no
opinion thereon.
14. However, we feel that since the original suit is of
the year 2018, an attempt should be made by the Trial
Court to conclude the suit expeditiously, so as to avoid
any further complication(s).
15. We, therefore, request the Trial Court to finally
hear and dispose of the two suits within a maximum period
of one year from today.
16. Accordingly,  Civil  Appeal  No.  12952 of  2026  is
disposed of.
17. For  the  reasons  mentioned  above,  Civil  Appeal
No(s).12953-12954 of 2026 are dismissed.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        of 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.13182/2026)
ANJNA SINGH      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Uday Gupta, learned Senior counsel
for the appellant; Mr. V.V.V. Pattabhiram, learned Deputy
Attorney  General  for  Respondent  No.1-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh; and Mr. Gopal Sankaranarayanan, learned Senior
counsel for Respondent No.2.
3. This appeal has been preferred by the informant
against the order dated 17.03.2026 passed by the High
Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at Jabalpur (briefly ‘the
High  Court’  hereinafter),  extending  the  benefit  of
anticipatory bail to Respondent No.2.
4. It is stated that Respondent No.2 has been named as
an  accused  along  with  others  in  Crime  No.485/2020
registered at Police Station- Civil Lines, District- Rewa,
Madhya Pradesh under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and 120B
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
5. The subject-matter of controversy is the estate of
late Vimla Singh, who is the mother of the appellant and
grandmother of Respondent No.2. More specifically, the
1

--- Page 211 ---
issue is regarding alleged forging of a Will stated to
have been authored by late Vimla Singh, bequeathing her
estate in favour of Respondent No.2. It is the allegation
of the informant-appellant that signature of late Vimla
Singh has been forged, with the needle of suspicion
pointing towards Respondent No.2, whose signature also
finds place in the Will.
6. The  High  Court  vide  the  impugned  order,  after
noticing that the dispute between the parties is of a
civil  nature  with  a  civil  suit  pending,  granted
anticipatory bail to Respondent No.2 with the conditions
mentioned in the impugned order.
7. Learned Senior counsel for the appellant submits that
the involvement of Respondent No.2 in the act of forgery
is evident, entailing serious consequences. It is not a
case where the High Court ought to have exercised the
discretion in favour of the accused. As a matter of fact,
the High Court itself records in paragraph 9 of the
impugned order that custodial interrogation of Respondent
No.2  may  be  required  for  taking  samples  of  his
handwriting, thumb impression etc. That apart, Respondent
No.2 is a resident of Germany. By granting anticipatory
bail,  the  entire  trial  has  been  jeopardized.  He,
therefore, seeks cancellation of the anticipatory bail
granted to Respondent No.2.
8. On the other hand, learned counsel for Respondent
No.1-State of Madhya Pradesh has referred to the counter
2

--- Page 212 ---
affidavit filed by Respondent No.1-State of Madhya Pradesh
and  submits  therefrom  that  the  State  Examiner  of
Questioned Documents, Government of Madhya Pradesh has
opined on 03.06.2022 that the questioned signatures of
late  Vimla  Singh  do  not  match  her  standard/admitted
signatures, thus scientifically establishing forgery. He
also submits that after Respondent No.2 left India for
Germany on 20.09.2019, he did not co-operate with or
appear before the investigating authorities for a long
time resulting in issuance of a Look-Out Circular. He
further submits that out of a total 06 accused, charge-
sheet No.292 of 2022 has been filed only against co-
accused Avinesh Pratap Singh and Naseem Ara. Further
investigation against the remaining 04 accused including
Respondent No.2 is going on. According to him, a strong
prima facie case has been established that the Will dated
01.12.2017 is a fabricated document, prepared and used by
Respondent No.2 to wrongfully deprive the appellant of her
legitimate share in the estate of late Vimla Singh.
9. Learned  Senior  counsel  for  Respondent  No.2  has
referred to the counter affidavit filed by him and submits
that already a civil suit has been instituted by the
appellant in respect of the same subject-matter which is
pending. Respondent No.2 has been arrayed as a defendant
in the civil suit. He submits that Respondent No.2 has not
even seen the contested Will till date. Referring to the
legal  opinion  tendered  by  the  Assistant  Director  of
3

--- Page 213 ---
Prosecution, Rewa dated 18.04.2026, which it is submitted
has been obtained through the Right to Information Act,
2005, he submits that Respondent No.2 had co-operated with
the  investigation  after  the  High  Court  in  a  writ
proceeding directed that no coercive action should be
taken against Respondent No.2. The Look-Out Circular has
also  been  cancelled  by  the  Bureau  of  Immigration.
Investigation  relating  to  Respondent  No.2  has  been
completed.  The  Assistant  Director  of  Prosecution  is
categorical in stating that Respondent No.2 has extended
full co-operation in the investigation.
10. We have given our anxious consideration to the rival
submissions made at the Bar and have also perused the
materials on record.
11. Though the dispute raised between the parties is
certainly  of  a  civil  nature,  elements  of  criminal
culpability or otherwise cannot be ruled out, at least at
this  stage.  However,  the  question  is  of  custodial
interrogation of Respondent No.2.
12. In  view  of  what  the  Assistant  Director  of
Prosecution, Rewa has opined and considering the fact that
anticipatory bail was granted to Respondent No.2 way back
on  17.03.2026,  we  are  not  inclined  to  cancel  the
anticipatory bail granted to Respondent No.2. However, we
direct that Respondent No.2 shall furnish an undertaking
that he would appear before the investigating agency as
and when required and certainly before the criminal court
4

--- Page 214 ---
on the dates of the trial. Such an undertaking shall be
furnished by Respondent No.2 before the Investigating
Officer within 15 days from today.
13. Subject to the above, the Criminal Appeal is disposed
of.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) No.8375/2024)
THE PRINCIPAL SECRETARY, COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRIES DEPARTMENT & ORS
..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
THE WORKMEN OF MYSORE PAPER MILLS 
LTD. & ANR.
..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Sanjay Hegde, learned senior counsel for the
appellant-State of Karnataka; Mr. Colin Gonsalves, learned senior
counsel for the workmen; and Mr. Siddarth Agarwal, learned counsel
for the management.
3. The workmen were engaged as forest watchers in the  Mysore
Paper Mills  which is a Government of Karnataka undertaking. An
industrial  dispute  arose  pursuant  to  which  the  appropriate
Government i.e., Government of Karnataka made a reference on
22.09.2005 under Section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act,
1947 to the Industrial Tribunal at Bangalore. The reference was
made on the following questions:
1.  Is  the  Mysore  Paper  Mills  Forest
Employees' Association, 5th Cross, Jail Road,
Channel's Left side, Shimoga District, Mysore
Paper Mills Forest Employees Union, Araga,
1

--- Page 232 ---
Thirthahally,  represented  by  its  General
Secretary justified in demanding M/s Mysore
Paper Mills Limited, Paper Town, Bhadravathi,
Shimoga District to regularise the services
of  529  Forest  Field  Watchers  (workmen)
mentioned  in  the  list  annexed  to  the
reference order? 
2. If not, to what relief the said workmen
are entitled?
4. The said reference was registered as A.I.D. No. 16 of 2005 and
was  heard  by  the  learned  Additional  Industrial  Tribunal  at
Bangalore (‘Industrial Tribunal’ hereinafter). By the order dated
25.07.2008, the Industrial Tribunal passed the following award:
AWARD
Though the Ist Party workmen have been engaged
by Mysore Paper Mills to work in Forest
Divisions, since prior to 1992, they are not
entitled for being absorbed against the posts
of Forest Plantation Watchers and Drivers.
They  are  entitled  for  wages  and  other
benefits  available  to  a  workman  under
Industrial Disputes Act and as provided from
time  to  time  under  settlement,  reached
between workmen and the IInd Party management.
5. The workmen assailed the aforesaid award before the High Court
of Karnataka at Bangalore (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) in
WP No.14012 of 2008 as well as in WP No.13284 of 2008. In the first
writ petition i.e., WP No.14012 of 2008, the State of Karnataka and
its concerned officials were arrayed as respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4.
The management also filed a writ petition assailing the award being
2

--- Page 233 ---
WP No.36195 of 2009. All the three writ petitions were heard
together and were disposed of by a common order dated 14.12.2022.
6. In the writ proceedings before the learned Single Judge,
learned counsel appearing for the workmen made a submission before
the writ court that the workmen would not press for regularization
or absorption of their service. Based on such submissions, learned
Single Judge framed the following question for determination:
Whether  the  members  of  the  petitioner
Association would be entitled to the same
wages as paid to Forest Watchers by the
Forest Department on the principle of equal
pay for equal work?
7. Ultimately, learned Single Judge while disposing of the three
writ petitions, set aside the award and directed the State of
Karnataka to make payment of wages to the workmen at the minimum of
pay-scale granted to the Forest Watchers employed by the Forest
Department, Government of Karnataka. Relevant portion of the order
dated 14.12.2022 is extracted hereunder:
ORDER
1.  W.P.Nos.14012/2008  and  13284/2008  are
partly allowed in terms of the answer to
point No.1.
a.  The  award  passed  by  the  Additional
Industrial  Tribunal,  Bengaluru  in  AID
No.16/2005 dated 25.07.2008 at Annexure-L is
quashed.
b. The Respondent State is directed to make
payment of wages (at the minimum of pay scale
at the lower cadre in the regular pay scale)
3

--- Page 234 ---
extended to the Forest Watchers employed by
the  Forest  Department  from  the  date  of
publication of Vidheyaka on 20.02.2018 till
date and going forward, in respect of the
persons named in the Vidheyaka unless they
having been superannuated.
c. The above payment to be made within a
period of three months from the date of
receipt of copy of this order.
d. The petitioner is permitted to serve a
copy on the respondents. In the event of the
respondents having any doubt about the order,
the QR code appended to the judgment could be
scanned  to  verify  the  authenticity  or
veracity of the judgment as also the contents
thereof.
e. It is made clear that there is no opinion
expressed  as  regards  the  regularization
and/or  absorption  of  the  members  of  the
petitioner-Union.
ii. W.P.Nos.36195/2009 is dismissed.
8. State of Karnataka being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of
the learned Single Judge dated 14.12.2022 preferred Writ Appeal
No.842 of 2023 before the Division Bench of the High Court. After
thorough consideration of all aspects of the matter, the Division
Bench dismissed the writ appeal  vide the impugned judgment and
order dated 03.01.2024 further granting a period of 3 months to the
State to comply with the directions of the learned Single Judge.
9. It is this order which has been impugned in the present
proceedings.
10. In the related Special leave petition, this Court had issued
4

--- Page 235 ---
notice vide order dated 15.04.2024 and had stayed the operation of
the impugned judgment and order dated 03.01.2024.
11. In the course of the hearing today, our attention has been
drawn to the Karnataka Daily Wage Employees Welfare Act, 2012. As
per the preamble to the aforesaid Act, the same has been enacted to
provide minimum security of tenure, better wages and certain social
securities  on  termination  from  long  public  service  to  those
category of daily wage employees who had rendered service for more
than 10 years. As per Section 3(1) of the aforesaid Act, the daily
wage employees in the establishments which would be notified by the
State Government under the aforesaid Act shall be continued on
daily wage basis till completion of 60 years of age. As per sub-
Section (2), the State Government was mandated to notify the names
of eligible daily wage employees of all establishments for the
purpose of sub Section (1) within one year from the date of
commencement of the Act.
11.1.  Section 4(1) of the Act specifically provides that the pay
of a daily wage employee within the ambit of the Act shall be the
minimum of the time scale of pay of the post in which he is
continued in service. He would also be entitled to various other
entitlements and leaves as may be determined by the Government from
time to time.
12. As per notification dated 20.02.2018, which has been revised
from time to time revising the pay scale of the workmen, issued by
the Ministry of Commerce and Industries, Government of Karnataka,
the daily wage employees who have worked in M/s. Mysore Paper Mills
Limited which came under the jurisdiction of the Commerce and
5

--- Page 236 ---
Industries Department for not less than 10 years and who were still
working, have been notified. This notification contains the names
of all the workmen of Mysore Paper Mills Limited whose industrial
dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. 
13. In the circumstances, we do not find any good ground to
interfere with the order of the learned Single Judge as well as the
impugned judgment and order of the Division Bench.
14. Accordingly, the Civil Appeal is dismissed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
......................J.
(UJJAL BHUYAN)
......................J.
(ATUL S. CHANDURKAR)
NEW DELHI;

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION No. 571 OF 2021
IN
(CIVIL APPEAL No. 2535 OF 2010)
NGEF EMPLOYEES HOUSE BUILDING SOCIETY    APPLICANT(S)/
    APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
SMT. MANGALAGOWRI       NON-APPLICANTS/
    RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard  Mr. Manjunath Meled,  learned counsel
for the applicant/appellant as well as Ms. Nidhi, learned
counsel for the respondent.
2. This Miscellaneous Application has been filed for
restoration of Civil Appeal No.2535 of 2010, which was
dismissed for non-prosecution on 03.03.2021.
3. On 14.08.2026, we had indicated that we would hear
the Miscellaneous Application along with the Civil Appeal.
4. As  per  office  report  dated  15.09.2026,  the
Miscellaneous Application was filed on 18.03.2021 for
restoration  of  the  Civil  Appeal,  dismissed  for  non-
prosecution. However, the same was not listed before the
Court.
5. We have also heard learned counsel for the parties in
1

--- Page 270 ---
the Civil Appeal. The related Special Leave Petition was
filed against the order dated 09.04.2009 passed by the
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi
(briefly  ‘the  Commission’  hereinafter),  rejecting  the
revision petition of the appellant. On 20.07.2009, notice
was issued and the impugned order of the Commission was
stayed.  Thereafter,  leave  was  granted  on  15.03.2010,
pursuant to which the case came to be registered as Civil
Appeal No.2535/2010.
6. Respondent is the widow of late B.R. Ramachandra, who
was a member of NGEF Employees House Building Society
(briefly  ‘the  society’  hereinafter),  i.e.  appellant
herein. Husband had sought for allotment of a site in the
layout of the society. It is stated that the society had
issued  no-objection  certificate  to  the  husband  on
15.05.1994 to either sell, mortgage or transfer the above
site  to  anybody  of  his  choice.  However,  possession
certificate was not issued. In this connection, reliance
was placed on a communication dated 04.04.2005 of the
society.
7. Following the death of the husband, respondent as the
complainant, instituted Complaint No.584 of 2008 before
the District Consumer Forum at Bengaluru, seeking the
following reliefs:
“a)  Direct  the  opponent  Society  to  issue
possession certificate in respect of a site
bearing No.36 at Chandra Layout, 1 st Stage,
Nrupathunga Nagar, Nagarbhavi, Bangalore which
2

--- Page 271 ---
was alloted the husband of the complainant and
to  register  the  same  in  the  name  of  the
complainant.”
8. Before the District Consumer Forum, appellant, i.e.
NGEF Employees House Building Society, did not contest the
proceedings by filing written statement or by tendering
evidence. Nonetheless, the District Forum declined to
entertain the complaint by holding that respondent failed
to prove and establish her case. She had also not filed
any criminal complaint. Accordingly, the complaint was
dismissed vide the order dated 29.04.2008.
9. In  appeal  before  the  Karnataka  State  Consumer
Disputes Redressal Commission (Appeal No.1686 of 2008),
the State Commission was of the opinion that it was a fit
case to issue direction to the appellant to execute and
register the sale deed in favour of the complainant.
Accordingly, the following order was passed:
“The complaint filed by the complainant before
the District Forum is allowed with a direction
to the Respondent/OP to execute the sale deed
in favour of the complainant, being wife of the
deceased Late Mr. B.R. Ramachandra, who was a
member of OP 1 society and register the same in
respect of the site bearing No.36 1 st stage
Chandra Layout, Bangalore within 3 months from
today.”
10. Appellant  challenged  this  order  dated  29.04.2008
before the Commission in Revision Petition No.874 of 2009.
The Revision Petition was dismissed vide the order dated
3

--- Page 272 ---
09.04.2009 in the following manner:
“ We find no infirmity in the order passed by
the State Commission. Learned Counsel appearing
for  the  petitioner  did  not  have  any
satisfactory explanation "As to why the written
statement  was  not  filed  by  the  petitioner
before the District Forum". It was submitted
before us that the NGEF, which is a public
undertaking of the State Government, has gone
in liquidation and the proceedings for its
winding up are pending before the High Court.
Petitioner,  which  is  an  Employees  House
Building Society, is not in liquidation. The
defence put up by the petitioner that since the
NGEF has gone in liquidation, all its papers
are lying with official liquidator/High Court,
cannot be accepted. The petitioner society, as
mentioned above, is not in liquidation and
consequently, its papers cannot be with the
official  liquidator/High  Court.  Revision
Petition is dismissed.”
11. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties, we
recall our order dated 03.03.2021 passed in Civil Appeal
No.2535 of 2010. The Civil Appeal is restored to its
original file and number, whereafter we have heard the
learned counsel for the parties in the Civil Appeal on
merits.
12. Accordingly,  the  Miscellaneous  Application
No.571/2021  is  allowed  and  all  pending  interlocutory
application(s) are disposed of.
13. On due consideration, we do not find any error or
4

--- Page 273 ---
infirmity  in  the  view  taken  by  the  Commission.  No
Interference is called for.
14. Consequently, Civil Appeal No.2535/2010 is dismissed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
…………………………………………………...J.
      
  [UJJAL BHUYAN]
…………………………………………………...J.
     [ATUL S. CHANDURKAR]
NEW DELHI;
16th SEPTEMBER, 2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
I.A. Nos. 93509/2026, 93506/2026, and 213528/2026
1. On an oral request by the counsel for the applicants, I.A. No.
213528/2026 is taken on board.
These applications have been moved for intervention, impleadment of
the State of Tamil Nadu as a party respondent, and to issue certain
directions, including a declaration that the applicants’ land is
not declared as a private forest in purported compliance with an
order dated 04.03.2025 passed by this Court in the instant Writ
Petition.
2. At the outset, we find that the proceedings pending before
this  Court  pertain  to  the  constitutionality  of  the  Forest
(Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 (“2023 Amendment”). Vide that
amendment, the definition of “forest” has been revised, and one of
the grounds to challenge the amended definition is that it runs
contrary to what this Court has held way back on 12.12.1996 in T.N.
Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India & Ors.  (W.P.(C) No. 202 of
1995).
3. On 04.03.2025, this Court took notice of various contentions
raised from both sides and referred to Rule 16 of the Van
(Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Rules, 2023 (for short, the “2023
Rules”), thereby directing that, based upon the definition of
3

--- Page 290 ---
“forest” as laid down by this Court in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad,
the State Governments and the Union Territories must identify the
boundaries of the forest areas. It was further held that, in terms
of the Rule 16(1), a consolidated record of such lands, including
the forest-like areas identified by the Expert Committee, be
prepared.
4. It seems that in purported compliance with the aforesaid
directions, some of the States have undertaken an exercise to
identify such forest lands/areas. We are not aware as to whether
the affected persons or those who are likely to be affected have
been granted an opportunity of being heard in this process or
whether an independent team of experts was assigned the task to
identify the forest lands/areas.
5. Be that as it may, the instant applications have been filed by
the applicants, who claim themselves to be absolute owners of land
measuring 59 Acres and 51.925 Cents in Village Kaliyal, Vilavancode
Taluk, Kanyakumari District, Tamil Nadu. Their case is that the
subject land is agricultural and plantation land, but in terms of
an old notification dated 31.12.1982, the District Collector has
declared it as a “private forest”.
6. While the facts would speak for themselves, it is difficult to
say whether the land of the applicants has been declared private
forest in purported compliance with the directions issued by this
Court or in deference to the apparently old notification dated
31.12.1982. It is further evident from the averments made in the
applications that the issue is pending consideration before the
Madras High Court in a Review Petition. That being so, we find no
4

--- Page 291 ---
ground to entertain these applications, which are accordingly
dismissed,  with  liberty  to  the  applicants  to  raise  their
contentions before the High Court in the pending Review Petition or
other appropriate proceedings. It is clarified that we have not
expressed any opinion with respect to the substance of the claim of
the applicants. The I.A.s are, accordingly, dismissed with the
liberty aforestated.
7. Having passed the above order in respect of the applicants’
case,  we  deem  it  appropriate  to  clarify  that  the  instant
proceedings are only confined to the constitutional validity of the
2023  Amendment.  At  this  stage,  it  is  neither  desirable  nor
expedient to expand the scope of the proceedings and thereby direct
identification of the forest areas in different States under the
supervision of this Court. Such an exercise, if so required, can be
overseen by the jurisdictional High Court(s), which are well-
equipped to determine such issues. That is especially so, when the
pre-amendment definition of forest land, as laid down by this Court
in  T.N.  Godavarman  Thirumulpad  (supra) , as well as the post-
amendment expression brought through the 2023 Amendment, can be
well understood and interpreted by the High Courts, keeping in view
the nature, geographical location, and any other relevant factor in
respect of lands that are sought to be included as or excluded from
the identification as forest land. The order dated 04.03.2025,
thus, stands clarified/modified to that extent.
IA No. 146216/2026
8. The Central Empowered Committee is directed to consider the
5

--- Page 292 ---
proposal of the applicant and submit its report.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.4559 of 2026
JAI PRAKASH SINGH                                  APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.                 RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Appellant, who was awarded M. Phil, Ph. D and D. Litt. degrees, was
at the material time holding the post of Reader (Associate Professor) in
the Department of Education, Dharam Samaj College, Aligarh, Uttar
Pradesh. He and Dr. Pradeep Kumar were appointed as Lecturer on the
same day, i.e., 15.3.1990. 
2. The respective pay drawn by the appellant and Dr. Pradeep Kumar
between 15.03.2000 and 15.03.2005 was as follows: 
S.No. Date of Salary Salary drawn by
the appellant
Salary drawn by
Dr.  Pradeep
Kumar
1. 15.03.2000 12420/- 12000/-
2. 15.03.2001 12840/- 12420/-
3. 15.03.2002 13260/- 12840/-
4. 15.03.2003 13680/- 13260/-
5. 15.03.2004 14100/- 13680/-
6. 15.03.2005 14520/- 14100/-
3. Dr. Pradeep Kumar had moved the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad1 by instituting a writ petition 2 for grant of benefit of two
advance increments as per provisions of Para 4(iv) of G.O. dated
1 High Court
2 Writ Petition No.26098 of 2008
1

--- Page 294 ---
16.02.1999. The High Court vide order dated 15.11.2011 directed grant of
two advance increment to Dr. Pradeep Kumar in pursuance of the Ph. D
degree awarded on 13.11.2002. 
4. In compliance with the said order, the Director of Education (Higher
Education), Uttar Pradesh 3, passed an order dated 20.06.2012 by which
the salary of Dr. Pradeep Kumar was fixed after adding two advance
increments and the net salary payable to Dr. Pradeep Kumar as on
01.07.2009 was fixed as Rs.53,513/-.
5. Though the appellant was senior to Dr. Pradeep Kumar, and had
obtained the degree of Ph. D in 1990 whereas Dr. Pradeep Kumar had
obtained the Ph. D degree in 2002, he started drawing higher pay than
the appellant. A representation dated 29.08.2012 was filed by the
appellant which was not answered. In pursuance of an order dated
19.12.20212 passed by the High Court on a writ petition, the appellant
filed a further representation dated 26.12.2012 which came to be rejected
by the Director on 14.03.2013.
6. Aggrieved by the Director’s order dated 14.03.2013, the appellant
had invoked the jurisdiction of the High Court again by presenting a writ
petition4. Appellant’s grievance was that since he was senior to Dr.
Pradeep Kumar and had obtained the Ph. D. degree much before him, his
pay should be at par with the pay being given to his junior. In the writ
petition, the appellant prayed as follows:
“(a) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of certiorari quashing
3 Director
4 Writ-A No.21228 of 2013
2

--- Page 295 ---
the impugned order dated 14.03.2013, passed by Respondent No.2
Director of Education (Higher Education), Allahabad (Annexure No.19 to
this Writ Petition)
(b) issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
commanding the Respondents to pay the salary to the Petitioner equal
to that of Dr. Pradeep Kumar, who is junior to the Petitioner from the
date the petitioner has become eligible alongwith the interest on the
arrears; 
***”
7.  Unfortunately, for the appellant, the High Court by a cryptic order
dated 08.05.2018, dismissed the writ petition. Such order is the subject
matter of challenge in this appeal by special leave granted on 15.04.2026
by a coordinate Bench. 
8. On the previous occasion, i.e. 01.09.2026, upon hearing learned
counsel for the appellant but in the absence of the respondents, we had
recorded a prima facie satisfaction that the appellant had been given a
raw deal. 
9. Today, Ms. Goel, learned standing counsel appearing for the State of
Uttar Pradesh has appeared. 
10. In support of the order under challenge and impugned in the writ
petition, Ms. Goel has invited our attention to Government Orders dated
16.02.1999, 01.12.1999 and 28.02.2009. According to Ms. Goel, the
appellant did not lay challenge to any of these Government Orders in
terms whereof the pay of Dr. Pradeep Kumar was fixed and, therefore, he
was rightly declined relief by the High Court.
11. We are afraid, the contention cannot be accepted.
12. Government Order dated 28.02.2009 specifically mandates as
follows:
3

--- Page 296 ---
“8. Any teacher who in the present prevalent pay scale in same cadre
is getting more salary in comparison to his junior teacher immediately
before date 1 January 2006 and in the revised pay scale if his salary is
fixed less than his junior teacher then the salary of the senior teacher
in the revised pay scale shall be made par with the salary of that junior
teacher.”
13. According to the High Court, paragraph 8 of the Government Order
dated 28.02.2009 would not be applicable to the appellant because he
was  not  drawing  higher  salary than  Dr.  Pradeep  Kumar  prior  to
01.01.2006. This appears to us to be an erroneous finding. The pay of Dr.
Pradeep Kumar was raised only after the order dated 15.11.2011 was
passed by the High Court on his writ petition. That apart, from the
aforesaid chart, it is clear that the appellant was drawing a higher pay
than Dr. Pradeep Kumar even before 01.01.2006.
14. Even otherwise, nothing much turns on the absence of challenge to
the Government Orders, referred to by Ms. Goel, by the appellant.
15. It is fundamental that a senior officer cannot be paid less than a
junior officer holding the same post. The position regarding fixation of pay
of the appellant and Dr. Pradeep Kumar is so grossly anomalous that the
same violates Article 14 of the Constitution of India as well as the
provisions in Article 39(d) of the Constitution. Undisputed facts are that
both the appellant as well as Dr. Pradeep Kumar were serving as Readers
in the Department of Education and that the appellant had obtained M.
Phil and Ph. D degrees prior to Dr. Pradeep Kumar obtaining the same. A
junior receiving a higher pay compared to the pay of the senior has to be
justified with reference to valid factors. No demonstrable difference in
4

--- Page 297 ---
qualifications  for  the  post,  source  of  recruitment,  experience,
responsibility and accountability is placed on record which could be
proffered as a justification for denying equal pay to the appellant for equal
work of equal value. The Government Orders, relied upon by Ms. Goel,
embody policy decisions of the Government; however, the same have to
yield to the over-arching principles of equality and equal pay for equal
work enshrined in the Constitution to the extent they are inconsistent
therewith. We, thus, see no valid reason to uphold the impugned order of
the High Court. The same stands set aside.
16. The appeal stands allowed. There shall be order in terms of the
prayer clauses in the writ petition, noted above in paragraph 6.
17. The financial benefits be made available to the appellant as early as
possible, but not later than three months from date.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No.4507 of 2026
(@Special Leave Petition (Crl) No.12967 of 2026)
Chitrank Upadhyay
....Appellant 
Versus
State of NCT of Delhi
 ….Respondent
O R D E R 
Leave granted.
2. The appellant is aggrieved with the summons produced as
Annexure P5, pursuant to the registration of FIR No. 263 of 2020
under Sections 188/269 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) dated
03.06.2020 registered at Vasant Kunj (North) Police Station, Delhi.
The allegations, as we see from the FIR was that a group of
students, in which the appellant was also a party, were carrying out
a demonstration and protest, when the police arrived at the spot
and informed them of an order under Section 144 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.PC). Some students fled and five were
detained.  The allegation was also that the appellant was not
wearing a mask. The prohibition order was issued at the initial
stages of COVID-19 pandemic as a measure to contain the spread of
the virus.    
3. COVID-19 has left its footprints everywhere and in this case by
the criminal prosecution initiated for violation of an order under

--- Page 300 ---
2
Section 144, Cr. PC.  We are not informed as to the subject matter of
the protest which was carried out by the students, though at an
inopportune moment, especially in the wake of the pandemic. The
youth faced with unpleasant realities of life, for reason of their sheer
innocence are bound to protest in anger and frustration. Their
feelings vented by way of demonstrations and slogan shouting is not
to be throttled or suppressed, but have to be channelised to bring
about a constructive change in society.  We are of the definite
opinion that the criminal prosecution of an incident that occurred in
2020, especially in the facts of the above case, is not liable to be
continued. 
4. We are not for a moment convinced by the legal contentions
raised of the written complaint having not been made by the officer
who passed the order.  Section 195(1)(a) of the Cr.PC mandates that
cognizance can be taken only when a complaint in writing is made
by the concerned public servant or one who is administratively
subordinate to that public servant. In the present case, Annexure P3
is a written complaint by the ACP itself, and he has authorised the
Sub-Inspector of Police who has given the First Information
Statement. No legal lacuna, vitiating the cognizance arose in the
above case, but still as we noticed, the students would have been
sufficiently  chastised,  especially  by  reason  of  the  pending

--- Page 301 ---
3
proceedings.  
5. We, hence, direct that no further proceedings be carried out in
pursuance of FIR No. 263 of 2020 under Sections 188/269 of the IPC
dated 03.06.2020 registered at Vasant Kunj (North) Police Station,
Delhi on which Annexure P5 summons was issued by the
Metropolitan Magistrate, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi. We make
it clear that the proceedings in its entirety shall stand quashed; not
only the appellant is absolved but also any other student who has
been implicated in the incident.
6. The appeal stands allowed. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.10449/2016
THE STATE OF U.P. FINANCE DEPARTMENT

VERSUS
OM PRAKASH TRIPATHI                 RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. The appeal is directed against the order dated 03 rd April, 2014 passed by
the Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad 1, whereby a writ
petition2 of the sole respondent was allowed with the following order:
“Having heard learned counsel for the parties and having
examined the records,  we are of the opinion that
respondents are under legal obligation to consider the
case of the petitioner for notional promotion for the post of
Director so that he may avail the benefits which may
become available to him after grant of such notional
promotion.
In view of the aforesaid, we dispose of the present writ
petition requiring the State Government to constitute a
departmental promotion committee and to consider the
claim of all such persons including the petitioner, who are
within the feeding cadre, in accordance with the rules
applicable for promotion on the post of Director, preferably
within three months from the date a certified copy of this
order is filed before respondent no. 1.
1  High Court
2  Writ - A No. - 5387 of 2011
1

--- Page 305 ---
With the aforesaid observation/direction the present writ
petition is disposed of.”
2. We have heard Mr. Ankit Goel, learned counsel appearing for the
appellants and Mr. Sunil Murarka, learned counsel who was appointed as amicus
curiae to represent the sole respondent at some length. 
3. Mr. Murarka, learned  amicus  curiae  has drawn our attention to a
supplementary counter-affidavit dated 13th December, 2013, which was filed in
course of the proceedings before the High Court. Paragraph 6 of such affidavit
reads as follows:
“….. 6. That  the  contents  of  paragraph  9  of  the
supplementary affidavit are not admitted and in reply it is
submitted that Court Lucknow Bench in Writ Petition No.
1389 (S/B) of 2007 related to consequential seniority and
reservation,  a  S.L.P.  has  been filed  before  Hon'ble
Supreme Court on which an order was passed on 28-02-
2011 for maintaining status-quo, and in consequence
thereof, no selection has been made by the Finance
Department, Government of U.P. on the post in Grade Pay
of Rs. 10,000 related to selection year 2010-11. After a
decision of the said S.L.P. by the Hon'ble Supreme Court
on 27.4.2012, a D.P.C. meeting under the chairmanship of
Chief Secretary was held on 4.7.2012 for making selection
of the aforesaid post in the pay scale of Rs. 18400-22400-
as revised in Pay Band-4, Rs. 37400-67000 and Grade Pay
Rs. 10,000 related to selection year 2010-11 and 2011-12.
Since the petitioner Om Prakash after attaining his age of
superannuation  has  been  retired  from  service  on
31.1.2011 and but in view of the Rules of department of
karmic, Govt. of U.P., the name of the petitioner has
already been included in the eligibility list of selection year
2010-11 at Sl. No. 5 but on the date of selection, he was
already  retired  from  service  and  as  such  no
2

--- Page 306 ---
recommendation was made by the selection committee in
favour of the petitioner which was in accordance with
rules. …..”
4. It is not in dispute that although at the material point of time there were
vacancies on the posts of Director, to which the respondent could have been
legitimately promoted upon his selection, promotion was accorded to three
officers belonging to the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe communities on the
basis of Rule 8A [introduced by way of an amendment in the Uttar Pradesh
Government Servants Seniority (Third Amendment) Rules, 2007].
5. However, consequent to such rule being challenged, it was outlawed by
the High Court and such decision of the High Court was also upheld by this
Court in the decision in Uttar  Pradesh  Power  Corporation  Limited  Vs.
Rajesh Kumar3.
6. It is, therefore, clear that but for Rule 8A, the respondent would not have
been superseded by the three officers belonging to Scheduled Caste/Scheduled
Tribe communities.
7. In such view of the matter and having regard to the fact that the
respondent could not be accorded promotion to the post of Director at an
appropriate time in terms of the selection made by the Departmental Promotion
Committee owing to his superannuation and he having no control over such
events, we see no reason to disturb the impugned order passed by the High
Court.  Accordingly, the appeal stands dismissed.
8. Be it noted that the respondent did not enter appearance before this
Court despite service, which led to Mr. Sunil Murarka’s engagement as amicus
3  (2012) 7 SCC 1
3

--- Page 307 ---
curiae. In the event, the respondent is alive, all benefits flowing from the
impugned order shall be accorded to him; if not, the benefits must be made
over to his heirs/legal representatives.
9. Appellants shall be under an obligation to release the benefits upon
making necessary enquiry within 3 months from date.
10. It is clarified that the order of the High Court shall be confined to the
respondent only and not read as a precedent for decision in future cases.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
